clue.text: Alert: Spanish uncle vanished with slip of the lip over my dead body

indicators.note: something that has vanished is no longer there, so those letters are taken out of the longer word

parts.note: an alert is a notification, as on a phone
tío is Spanish for uncle

indicators.note: a slip is a stumble or mix-up, so the words that follow come out in a jumbled order

parts.note: taken as written, ready to be mixed up

explanation.surface: A warning about a vanished uncle in Spain, given by someone stubbornly refusing.
explanation.walkthrough: Take TIO out of NOTIFICATION to leave NOTIFICAN, then add a jumble of THE LIP: NOT IF I CAN HELP IT.
explanation.definitionFit: Both are emphatic idioms of refusal, saying the speaker will prevent something happening at all costs.

clue.text: Singer, for example, with a number on live record

parts.note: No. is the abbreviation for number
to be is to live or exist
a list is a written record

explanation.surface: A vocalist with a song on a live album.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Singer' suggests a vocalist, but it is the writer Isaac Bashevis Singer.
explanation.definitionFit: Isaac Bashevis Singer won the 1978 Nobel Prize in Literature, making him an example of a prizewinner of that award.

clue.text: Arrange to plead for slippery youngster?

indicators.note: to arrange is to put into a fresh order, so the letters are reordered

parts.note: taken as written, then rearranged

explanation.surface: A lawyer arranging to plead on behalf of a shifty young client.
explanation.walkthrough: The question mark flags the playful definition: a young frog is literally slippery.
explanation.definitionFit: A tadpole is a juvenile frog or toad, a slimy little creature.

clue.text: Oral disease moved quickly

indicators.note: oral means spoken by mouth, so the word counts by how it is said

parts.note: influenza, a common disease, said out loud

explanation.surface: A mouth infection that spread fast.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Oral disease' looks like one thing, a complaint of the mouth, but 'Oral' is the sound signal.
explanation.definitionFit: Flew is the past tense of fly, which also means to go fast.

clue.text: I teach pal mysterious Muslim rule

indicators.note: something mysterious is puzzling and obscure, so the letters are scrambled out of their plain order

parts.note: taken as written, then rearranged

explanation.surface: A tutor tells a friend about an enigmatic religious law.
explanation.definitionFit: A caliphate is the realm or reign of a caliph, an Islamic ruler.

clue.text: Aware, naked, and hopeless

indicators.note: naked means stripped bare, so the word loses its outer letters

parts.note: knowing means aware

explanation.surface: Someone conscious, unclothed and in despair.
explanation.walkthrough: The clue reads like a list of three states, but 'naked' tells you to strip KNOWING of its first and last letters.
explanation.definitionFit: A no-win situation is one that cannot turn out well, so it is hopeless.

clue.text: Symbol pinned to your ear is a critical feature of many conversations

definitions.text: a critical feature of many conversations

indicators.note: what reaches the ear is sound, so the words are judged by how they are spoken

parts.note: a symbol is an icon, and pinned means tacked; said together they run into the grid phrase

explanation.surface: A badge pinned beside your ear that matters in many conversations.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Pinned to your ear' suggests an earring or badge, but 'to your ear' is the sound signal.
explanation.definitionFit: Looking someone in the eyes while talking is widely seen as essential to engaged communication.

clue.text: Exercise regimen for Pontius and his family?

definitions.meaning: first meaning: a fitness system of core-strengthening moves
second meaning: the household of Pontius Pilate, named as a family the way one speaks of the Joneses

explanation.walkthrough: The question mark flags the whimsical second meaning: a family called Pilate would be the Pilates.
explanation.definitionFit: The fitness system is named after Joseph Pilates, and the plural of the governor's surname spells the same.

clue.text: Spanish performer, ripped or flipped

parts.note: tore means ripped

indicators.note: flipped means turned over end to end, so that short word is read backwards

parts.note: taken as written, then read backwards

explanation.surface: A Spanish entertainer whose costume was either torn or turned upside down.
explanation.definitionFit: A torero is a bullfighter, who performs in the Spanish bullring.

clue.text: Fed reorganized, amid loud call for strange political ally?

indicators.note: amid means in the middle of, so one piece sits inside the other

parts.note: a bellow is a loud shout

indicators.note: reorganizing puts things into a new order, so these letters are rearranged

parts.note: taken as written, then mixed up

explanation.surface: The Federal Reserve gets reorganized amid shouting about odd political partnerships.
explanation.walkthrough: The definition plays on the saying 'politics makes strange bedfellows', hence the question mark.
explanation.definitionFit: From the proverb 'politics makes strange bedfellows': an unlikely partner thrown together with you by circumstance.

clue.text: Mathematician's error breaking rule

indicators.note: breaking something smashes it apart, so its letters are rearranged along with the extra one

parts.note: E is the baseball scorer's abbreviation for an error
taken as written

explanation.surface: A mathematician slips up and breaks one of the rules.
explanation.walkthrough: The 's is short for 'is', joining the definition to the wordplay; E for error comes from baseball box scores.
explanation.definitionFit: Leonhard Euler was the prolific eighteenth-century Swiss mathematician.

clue.text: Circle swimming hole the other way

indicators.note: going the other way means travelling in the opposite direction, so the word is read from its end

parts.note: a swimming hole is a pool

explanation.surface: Someone does laps around a swimming hole in the opposite direction.
explanation.definitionFit: A loop is a closed curve, a ring shape like a circle.

clue.text: Uniformed students overdose on drinks, backing up propagandist

indicators.note: backing up means moving backwards, so the string of pieces is read in the opposite direction

parts.note: the Reserve Officers' Training Corps, US college students in military uniform
standard abbreviation
nips are small drinks of spirits

explanation.surface: Cadets overdose on drinks, egged on by a propagandist.
explanation.walkthrough: ROTC is the US college officer-training program.
explanation.definitionFit: A spin doctor is a press agent who puts a favorable slant on news: a modern propagandist.

clue.text: Bone and grain maintaining Turkic population

indicators.note: maintaining means holding or keeping, so the first piece holds the second inside it

parts.note: meal is coarsely ground grain
the Tatars are a Turkic people of Russia and Central Asia

explanation.surface: Bones and cereal keeping a Central Asian people alive.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Bone and grain' reads as a pair of foods; 'Bone' alone is the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: A metatarsal is one of the five long bones of the foot.

clue.text: Heard (perceived) part of show

indicators.note: something heard is taken in by the ear, so the word is judged by its sound rather than its spelling

parts.note: perceived means seen, and it is pronounced the same as the word in the grid

explanation.surface: A remark that one part of a show was heard and noticed.
explanation.walkthrough: The brackets just set the wordplay word apart for the surface reading.
explanation.definitionFit: A scene is a section of a play, film or other performance.

clue.text: Engineer dictates conclusive assessment

indicators.note: to engineer is to construct or contrive, so the letters are rebuilt into something new

parts.note: taken as written, then rearranged

explanation.surface: An engineer lays down the law about what counts as a final evaluation.
explanation.definitionFit: An acid test is a decisive trial, from testing gold with nitric acid.

clue.text: Highly concentrated incentive discussed after trade

indicators.note: a trade is an exchange, so two letters of the word swap places
something discussed is talked about, so the result counts by its spoken sound

parts.note: swap the C and the T of the word for a motivation, then say the result

explanation.surface: A powerful motivation talked over after a business deal.
explanation.walkthrough: Swapping the C and T in INCENTIVE gives INTENCIVE, which sounds exactly like INTENSIVE.
explanation.definitionFit: Intensive means focused and concentrated on a small area or short period, as in intensive care or study.

clue.text: Mad, steep chaos!

indicators.note: chaos is utter disorder, so the preceding letters are thrown into a new order

parts.note: taken as written, then rearranged

explanation.surface: An exclamation at frenzied, headlong pandemonium.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Mad' looks like the anagram signal, but it is part of the letters; 'chaos' does the mixing, and the whole clue describes a frantic rush.
explanation.definitionFit: A stampede is a frenzied headlong rush of a herd or crowd, a scene of mad chaos.

clue.text: Exceedingly shoddy mimic in box

indicators.note: in places one piece inside the other, the way something is put inside a box

parts.note: a chest is a large box
to ape is to imitate

explanation.surface: A trashy imitation turns up packed in a box.
explanation.definitionFit: Cheapest is the superlative of cheap in its sense of poor-quality, so it means shoddy to the highest degree.

clue.text: Carefully conserve a set of cards securing computer connection

indicators.note: securing means holding firmly, so the first piece encloses the second

parts.note: a hand is the set of cards a player holds
a USB port connects devices to a computer

explanation.surface: Guard a deck of cards carefully while plugging in a computer cable.
explanation.definitionFit: To husband resources is to manage them thriftily so that they last.

clue.text: Third of December: frightful date for military trainee

indicators.note: third of points at a single letter, the one in third place of the following word

parts.note: the third letter of the month's name

indicators.note: frightful suggests something hideously disordered, so the following word is scrambled

parts.note: taken as written, then mixed up

explanation.surface: The third of December was a dreadful date for a young recruit.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Third of December' looks like a calendar date, but it asks for a letter of the word.
explanation.definitionFit: A cadet is a young person in training to become an officer in the armed forces.

clue.text: Head of livestock entrusted to brave pet

indicators.note: something entrusted to another is placed in their keeping, so it goes inside the other piece

parts.note: daring means brave

indicators.note: the head is the top, which in a word is its first letter

parts.note: its opening letter

explanation.surface: A head of cattle left in the care of a fearless pet.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Pet' seems to be an animal in the farm picture; here it is a term of endearment.
explanation.definitionFit: Pet and darling are both affectionate names for a favorite or a loved one.

clue.text: Phase originally boosting runner!

indicators.note: originally means at the start, so only the opening letter is wanted

parts.note: its opening letter

indicators.note: to boost is to lift up, and in a down entry lifting a word means reading it from bottom to top

parts.note: a miler is a runner who races over a mile

explanation.surface: An early stage of the competition gives an athlete a lift.
explanation.walkthrough: Read whole, the clue describes the answer: a qualifying heat is the opening phase that helps a runner up into the final.
explanation.definitionFit: A prelim is a preliminary round or heat, the stage that sends a runner on toward the final.

clue.text: Diner with lounge atmosphere, not excluding oxygen

indicators.note: excluding means leaving out, so a letter is dropped from the word before it

parts.note: to lounge is to rest
an aura is a distinctive atmosphere
taken as written
O is the chemical symbol for oxygen

explanation.surface: A diner with the feel of a cocktail lounge, though not short of air.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Not excluding' reads like a double negative meaning including, but it is NOT with its O removed. 'Diner' looks like a person eating; here it is the place.
explanation.definitionFit: In American usage a diner is an inexpensive eating place, a kind of restaurant.

clue.text: Barbie nearly failing as congregation's leader

indicators.note: failing suggests falling apart, so the remaining letters collapse into a new order
nearly means not quite all, so the word loses its last letter

parts.note: the doll's name, taken as written

explanation.surface: A Barbie doll on the verge of collapse serving as a religious leader.
explanation.definitionFit: A rabbi is the spiritual leader of a Jewish congregation.

clue.text: Formal park boundary

parts.note: P is the abbreviation for park, as on road signs
a rim is an edge or boundary

explanation.surface: The edge of a park laid out in a stiff, ceremonial style.
explanation.definitionFit: Prim means stiffly proper and correct, much like formal in manner.

clue.text: British comic is an object of worship in audio recording

indicators.note: an audio recording carries only sound, so the word is identified by how it is spoken

parts.note: an idol is something worshipped, pronounced the same as the grid word

explanation.surface: A British comedian is adored on a sound recording.
explanation.walkthrough: Eric Idle is the British comedian from Monty Python.
explanation.definitionFit: Eric Idle, a founding member of Monty Python, is a celebrated English comedian.

clue.text: A large quantity of boys grabbing ring

indicators.note: grabbing means taking hold of, so the first piece wraps around the second

parts.note: lads are boys
the letter O is ring-shaped

explanation.surface: Plenty of boys making a grab for a ring.
explanation.definitionFit: Loads is the informal noun for a great amount, as in loads of time.

clue.text: 50 imprisoned in chains with incomplete plan to deliver a nasty surprise

indicators.note: someone imprisoned is shut inside, so one piece goes within the other

parts.note: to chain someone is to bind them; binds are fetters
L is the Roman numeral for fifty

indicators.note: incomplete means lacking its end, so the last letter of the word that follows is cut

parts.note: an idea is a plan

explanation.surface: Fifty prisoners in chains with a half-finished escape plan, out to spring a surprise.
explanation.definitionFit: To blindside is to catch someone unawares, hitting them from where they cannot see it coming.

clue.text: Compilation of letters from maligned YA author

indicators.note: a compilation gathers material together, so the answer is assembled using only the letters found in the next word

parts.note: its eight distinct letters are the only ones the answer uses, several of them more than once
a letter of the word, reused as often as needed

explanation.surface: An anthology of correspondence from a much-criticized young-adult novelist.
explanation.walkthrough: This is an unusual device: every letter of MADELEINE L'ENGLE comes from MALIGNED, and every letter of MALIGNED is used, but with repeats, so it is not a straight anagram.
explanation.definitionFit: Madeleine L'Engle wrote A Wrinkle in Time, a classic of young-adult fiction.
